implementation_notes: The C++17 parallel overloads take an execution policy, so the standard library owns the decomposition: std::sort(std::execution::par, v.begin(), v.end()) or std::reduce(std::execution::par_unseq, ...) splits, balances and joins internally, and the program writes no recursion at all. par allows the element-access calls to run in threads the library creates; par_unseq relaxes them to unordered, unsequenced execution and forbids synchronising operations (locks, atomics) inside them. Hand-written recursion remains the right form when the decomposition carries data the algorithms cannot express (custom combine, tree shapes, memoisation); the toolchain must supply or link a parallel backend, since a standard library without one silently runs the algorithm sequentially.
pitfalls: par_unseq forbids synchronising operations inside user callbacks (no mutexes, no atomics) and permits unordered, unsequenced invocation - comparators and predicates must be pure.
Without a parallel backend linked in, the policy degrades to sequential execution: measure before claiming a speedup.
Small inputs get slower under par because the scheduling overhead dominates; keep a size threshold around the parallel call.

variants.name: std::async / std::future fork-join
variants.implementation_notes: C++11 gives the forks without the pool: each std::async(std::launch::async, fn, args) starts its callable on a new thread of execution and the returned std::future joins it through get(), so a recursive split becomes two async calls plus one combine. The cost is that nesting std::async at every level starts a thread per level - bound the recursion depth or push the subproblems onto an explicit pool (std::thread::scope, a hand-written task queue, or a library scheduler) before this variant pays off. Choose it for a shallow, bounded decomposition or for one-off background work rather than for a wide recursion.
pitfalls: std::async without std::launch::async may run the callable lazily inside get(): the recursion silently serialises.
One nested async per recursion level creates a thread per subproblem; bound the depth or use an explicit pool.
Exceptions surface at get(), not at the async call - a branch that throws must be joined before the caller returns, or the failure is lost.
